questions.q: What was the first trade union established in India, who founded it, and in which year?
questions.a: The first trade union in India was established in April 1918 in Madras by B.P. Wadia, a social worker and member of the Theosophical Society. A wrong answer (e.g., naming AITUC as the first union, or attributing it to Gandhi) reveals the student conflates the first union with the first *national* federation, or confuses the Textile Labour Association (founded by Gandhi in 1918) with Wadia's Madras Labour Union.

questions.q: Explain why the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) split in 1947 and what new organisation was formed as a result.
questions.a: The AITUC split in 1947 because the Indian National Congress, uncomfortable with growing communist control over AITUC (led by S.A. Dange and M.N. Roy), formed a rival federation — the Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) — in May 1947. A wrong answer (e.g., attributing the split to ideological differences alone, or saying INTUC was formed by communists) shows the student misses the political-party-driven nature of Indian trade unionism: unions have historically been extensions of political parties, not autonomous worker organisations.

questions.q: The Bombay Textile Strike of 1981-82 involved approximately 2.5 lakh workers and lasted over 18 months. Apply the concept of 'political-party-driven unionism' to explain why the strike failed despite massive participation.
questions.a: The strike failed because: (1) The Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh (RMMS), the recognised union affiliated to Congress/INTUC, was seen as colluding with mill owners; (2) Rival unions (communist-affiliated, socialist-affiliated) fragmented worker unity; (3) The state used the Essential Services Maintenance Act (ESMA) and police repression; (4) Mill owners, facing structural unviability, used the strike as pretext for permanent closure. A wrong answer focusing only on "worker disunity" or "state repression" misses the structural shift: the strike marked the end of the post-Independence social compact where the state mediated labour-capital relations through recognised unions.

questions.q: Compare the colonial-era worker protests (pre-1920) with the post-1947 institutionalised trade union phase on THREE dimensions: organisation, ideology, and relationship with the nationalist movement.
questions.a:
| Dimension | Colonial-era (pre-1920) | Post-1947 Institutionalised Phase |
|-----------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Organisation | Spontaneous, localised, no formal structure | Formal federations (AITUC, INTUC, HMS, UTUC), recognised unions, collective bargaining |
| Ideology | Economic grievances (wages, conditions), no coherent ideology | Explicitly ideological: communist, socialist, nationalist, Gandhian — each tied to a political party |
| Nationalist movement | Nationalist leaders (Gandhi, Tilak) *drew workers in* (e.g., 1917 Bombay strikes, Ahmedabad 1918) | Unions *became arms of political parties*; INTUC = Congress, AITUC = CPI, HMS = Socialists — worker autonomy subordinated to party politics |

A wrong answer that treats both phases as "same but bigger" misses the qualitative shift from *moral economy* protests to *political-party-controlled* interest-group politics.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The 1974 railway strike was the last major offensive by the organised working class in India; after that, the workers' movement entered a defensive, fragmented phase." Support your evaluation with evidence from the trajectory of trade unionism.
questions.a: The claim is largely accurate. The 1974 railway strike (led by George Fernandes, 1.7 million workers) was a high-water mark of organised labour's offensive capacity — it challenged the state directly during the Emergency prelude. After 1974: (1) The 1981-82 Bombay Textile Strike ended in catastrophic defeat and deindustrialisation; (2) Liberalisation (1991) accelerated informalisation — today >90% workforce is informal, outside union coverage; (3) Unions fragmented further along party lines, unable to organise contract/casual workers; (4) New labour struggles (e.g., Maruti Suzuki 2011-12, gig worker protests) are spontaneous, leaderless, and lack legal recognition. A wrong answer that says "unions are still strong" ignores the structural decline in union density, collective bargaining coverage, and the shift from 'class-based' to 'identity/fragmented' struggles.

questions.q: Create a conceptual map showing how the Bombay Textile Strike (1981-82) connects to THREE contemporary 'new labour struggles' in India. For each connection, name the struggle, the structural cause linking them, and the new form of organisation (if any).
questions.a: (1) The Maruti Manesar struggle — contractualisation replacing permanent jobs, the same structural force as the Bombay strike's substitute-labour system, met by workers building committees outside recognised unions, (2) Gig workers' protests — platform capitalism managing informal labour through algorithms, answered by app-based collectives that mobilise digitally, (3) Scheme workers' movements — the state outsourcing welfare functions to nominally volunteer helpers on honorariums, challenged by federations demanding recognition as workers with a minimum wage, (4) The connecting thread — informalisation, contractualisation and state withdrawal link the 1982 defeat to today's struggles, and each new struggle invents organisation beyond the traditional union. A poor answer lists random strikes without identifying the structural continuity or the organisational innovation.
